ch19.anchor: the Fourth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party opened in Shanghai
ch19.note: The Fourth Plenum (January 1931) is remembered as the moment the Moscow-trained group around Wang Ming (Chen Shaoyu) seized the Party leadership, with the backing of the Comintern delegate Pavel Mif; the “Left” line it installed dominated the Party until the Zunyi conference of 1935. Corroborated. Wang Ming and Mif are treated in the note to chapter 2.

ch19.anchor: Zhang Guotao, Shen Zemin, and Chen Changhao to the Hubei-Henan-Anhui border
ch19.note: The Hubei-Henan-Anhui (E-Yu-Wan) Soviet, straddling the three provinces around the Dabie Mountains, was the second-largest Communist base of the early 1930s and became the home of the Fourth Front Army. Under Zhang Guotao’s leadership its main force was driven out in 1932, as Mu Xin relates. Corroborated. Zhang Guotao is treated in the notes to chapters 1 and 5.

ch19.anchor: Gu Shunzhang turned traitor at once
ch19.note: Gu Shunzhang’s defection in April 1931 is among the best-documented disasters of the early Communist underground. Arrested in Hankou on 24 April, he offered to change sides at once; his knowledge of the Shanghai apparatus led over the following months to the deaths of a great many Communists. What limited the damage was the warning from the Party’s agent inside Xu Enzeng’s office, Qian Zhuangfei (chapter 5). Independent scholarship corroborates the arrest, the defection, and Qian Zhuangfei’s warning to Zhou Enlai. Gu Shunzhang himself is introduced in chapter 9.

ch19.anchor: There was at the time in Wuhan a certain Wang Zhuqiao, who had been arrested and turned traitor
ch19.note: Author’s note. Accounts differ on whether the informer who spotted Gu Shunzhang was Wang Zhuqiao or You Chongxin. At a 1979 discussion of the Central Special Section, the veterans Li Qiang, Liu Ding, Chen Yangshan, and Ke Lin held it was Wang Zhuqiao; Li Qiang said in 1981 that in Shanghai they had been told Gu Shunzhang was discovered by Wang Zhuqiao, though some accounts name You Chongxin, and the two may be one man under two names, or both may have had a hand in it. This translation follows the usage of earlier works in writing the informer as Wang Zhuqiao.

ch19.anchor: the third volume of My Recollections
ch19.note: Zhang Guotao broke with the Party and defected to the Kuomintang in 1938; his three-volume memoir My Recollections (Wo de huiyi) was written in exile and published in Hong Kong in the 1960s. It is a hostile source on much of Party history, but on this journey—which Mu Xin quotes at length—its account squares with the Communist record.

ch19.anchor: the dozen-odd passengers were all "yellow-fish" the sailors were smuggling aboard on the side
ch19.note: “Yellow-fish” (huangyu) was river-boat slang for passengers a crew smuggled aboard privately, off the books, for a fee.

ch19.anchor: later described Gu Shunzhang's arrest and defection like this
ch19.note: Author’s note. The passage is from Cai Mengjian, “The Story of Two Men Who Might Have Rewritten Modern Chinese History,” in Biographical Literature (Zhuanji wenxue, Taipei), vol. 37, no. 5, November 1980. Cai Mengjian, the Kuomintang officer who took Gu’s surrender, is also treated in the note to chapter 5.

ch19.anchor: I have been trained by the Soviet GPU
ch19.note: The GPU (later OGPU) was the Soviet state security and intelligence service of the 1920s and 1930s, forerunner of the NKVD and KGB. Gu’s boast of GPU training refers to a course he had taken in the Soviet Union.

ch19.anchor: A lifetime's wit, a whole body's daring; Duke Zhou breaks the foe's plot with a laugh
ch19.note: The couplet (Yi sheng jizhi yi shen dan, Zhou gong tanxiao po di mou) is a later popular tribute to Zhou Enlai’s handling of the Gu Shunzhang crisis; “Duke Zhou” puns on Zhou Enlai’s surname and the ancient statesman the Duke of Zhou.

ch20.note: Yun Daiying (1895–1931) was among the most influential Communist youth organizers of the 1920s—editor of China Youth and a political instructor at the Whampoa Academy. Betrayed by Gu Shunzhang, he was executed at the Nanjing Central Military Prison on 29 April 1931. Independent scholarship corroborates the identification through Gu’s confession and the execution. His earliest appearance in this book is noted in chapter 2.

ch20.anchor: he suddenly ran into an enemy "shakedown search."
ch20.note: Author’s note. Under Kuomintang rule, chao bazi (“shakedown search”) was the term for police and patrolmen stopping passers-by in the street to search them.

ch20.anchor: and the League of Left-Wing Writers authors Hu Yepin and Rou Shi
ch20.note: The killings of 7 February 1931 at the Longhua garrison in Shanghai—of some two dozen Communists seized at a secret meeting in January—are commemorated as the Longhua Martyrs. Among them were the “Five Martyrs of the League of Left-Wing Writers”: Rou Shi, Hu Yepin, Yin Fu, Feng Keng, and Li Weisen (Li Qiushi). Independent accounts confirm the date and the executions (by shooting, or by some accounts burial alive); sources give the total as twenty-three or twenty-four.

ch20.anchor: keeping my ardor whole, to play the captive of Chu
ch20.note: “Captive of Chu” (Chu qiu) is a classical allusion, from the Zuo Commentary, to a prisoner who keeps his dignity and loyalty in captivity; here Yun Daiying casts himself as such a captive.

ch20.anchor: even his student Huang Jingwen, who knew him well, could scarcely make him out
ch20.note: Author’s note. This and the further prison passages below are from Zhang Yu and Tie Feng, A Life of Yun Daiying (Yun Daiying zhuan), China Youth Press, 1995.

ch20.anchor: an outstanding early leader of the Chinese Communist Party and a brilliant Marxist theorist
ch20.note: Cai Hesen (1895–1931), a founder of the Party and its early theorist, was betrayed by Gu Shunzhang at a Hong Kong seamen’s meeting on 10 June 1931, extradited to the Guangdong warlord Chen Jitang, and executed in Guangzhou; independent records date his death to 4 August 1931, aged 36. The manner of execution given here—his limbs nailed to a wall and his chest run through with a bayonet—is the account of Communist sources and is not independently corroborated. His earliest appearance is noted in chapter 11.

ch20.anchor: In early 1928 Cai Hesen's wife Xiang Jingyu was arrested in Wuhan
ch20.note: Xiang Jingyu (1895–1928), Cai Hesen’s wife, was among the foremost women of the early Party and the first head of its women’s department; she was arrested and executed in Wuhan in 1928.

ch20.anchor: the address of Xiang Zhongfa, then general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party
ch20.note: Xiang Zhongfa (1880–1931), a former Wuhan dockworker, was made the Party’s nominal general secretary at the Sixth Congress of 1928 on the Comintern’s insistence that a worker head the Party. He remains the only CCP general secretary to defect to the enemy: arrested on 22 June 1931 on Gu Shunzhang’s information, he confessed at once and was shot on the 24th, before a stay of execution from Chiang Kai-shek could reach his jailers. Independent scholarship corroborates the arrest, the defection, and the execution. His earliest appearance is noted in the preface.

ch20.anchor: When the Comintern secretary Bukharin gave his report
ch20.note: Nikolai Bukharin (1888–1938), a leading Soviet theorist, headed the Comintern from 1926 to 1929; he was later ousted by Stalin and executed after the last of the Moscow show trials in 1938.

ch20.anchor: after the 'January 28' of 1932, the Kuomintang let him out
ch20.note: The “January 28 Incident” was the Japanese assault on Shanghai that began on 28 January 1932 and the resistance the Nineteenth Route Army put up against it; the turmoil it caused is what let Bao Junfu be released.

ch20.anchor: After the nationwide campaign to suppress counter-revolutionaries began in October 1950
ch20.note: The Campaign to Suppress Counter-revolutionaries (zhenfan) of 1950–1953 was a mass drive against former Kuomintang officials, secret agents, landlords, and others deemed enemies of the new state; several hundred thousand people were executed.

ch20.anchor: he died suddenly of a heart attack
ch20.note: Qincheng Prison, near Beijing, is China’s highest-security political prison, built in the late 1950s; that Bao Junfu could live in a house on its grounds with “fairly free movement,” as Li Qiang notes, marks his unusual, protected status even under detention.
